claims.claim: The wound healing defect in vimentin-deficient larvae was wound-specific, as unwounded morphants did not display a defect in fin length or area compared to age matched controls during normal development.
claims.source: This defect was wound-specific, as unwounded morphants did not display a defect in fin length or area compared to age matched controls during normal development (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F–H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by measurements of unwounded larvae shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F-H.

claims.claim: The wound healing defect in vimentin-deficient zebrafish larvae is consistent with the wound defect reported in VIM-/- mice.
claims.source: These findings are consistent with the wound defect reported with VIM-/- mice (Cheng et al., 2016; Eckes et al., 2000; Menko et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim cites three studies (Cheng et al., 2016; Eckes et al., 2000; Menko et al., 2014) for comparison.

claims.claim: Vimentin-deficient larvae displayed no defect in the appearance of vim+ cells at the wound edge following amputation.
claims.source: It should also be noted that vimentin-deficient larvae displayed no defect in the appearance of vim+ cells at the wound edge following amputation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), indicating that vimentin is not required for the activation of the vimentin promoter along the wound edge.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: Vimentin is not required for the activation of the vimentin promoter along the wound edge.
claims.source: It should also be noted that vimentin-deficient larvae displayed no defect in the appearance of vim+ cells at the wound edge following amputation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), indicating that vimentin is not required for the activation of the vimentin promoter along the wound edge.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that vimentin-deficient larvae still show vim+ cells at the wound edge.

claims.claim: Vimentin-deficient larvae showed no defect in apoptosis at 1 hpw as indicated by TUNEL staining.
claims.source: To determine if the regenerative defect was due to effects on cell survival, we assessed apoptosis by TUNEL staining. No defect was observed in the vimentin-deficient larvae at 1 hpw (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), providing evidence that the wound healing defect is likely not due to changes in cell survival.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by TUNEL staining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: The wound healing defect in vimentin-deficient larvae is likely not due to changes in cell survival.
claims.source: To determine if the regenerative defect was due to effects on cell survival, we assessed apoptosis by TUNEL staining. No defect was observed in the vimentin-deficient larvae at 1 hpw (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), providing evidence that the wound healing defect is likely not due to changes in cell survival.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of apoptosis defect in vimentin-deficient larvae.

claims.claim: Co-injection of vimentin MO1 and zebrafish vimentin RNA was sufficient to rescue the regeneration defect observed in the morphants.
claims.source: To confirm that the regeneration defect was not due to off-target effects of the MO, we rescued vimentin expression using co-injection of vimentin MO1 and zebrafish vimentin RNA and also used a second MO (MO2) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E). Co-injection was sufficient to rescue the regeneration defect observed in the morphants, suggesting that vimentin is required for fin regeneration in zebrafish (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A-C.

claims.claim: Vimentin is required for fin regeneration in zebrafish.
claims.source: Co-injection was sufficient to rescue the regeneration defect observed in the morphants, suggesting that vimentin is required for fin regeneration in zebrafish (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–C).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the rescue experiment results.

claims.claim: Mosaic F0 vimentin mutants generated using CRISPR-Cas9 displayed reduced regenerate length at 3 dpw.
claims.source: As further confirmation that vimentin is required for optimal wound healing, we used CRISPR-Cas9 mutagenesis to create mosaic F0 vimentin mutants. The CRISPR was validated by TOPO cloning and sequencing of individual F0 larvae as well as by sequencing germline DNA isolated from F0 adults (Figure 3C–E). The mosaic F0 mutants also displayed reduced regenerate length and area at 3 dpw (Figure 3F,G, Figure 3—figure supplement 3D, Figure 3—source data 2) but had no developmental defect in fin length (Figure 3—figure supplement 3E–G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by CRISPR-Cas9 mutagenesis data shown in Figure 3F, 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 3D, and Figure 3—source data 2.

claims.claim: Mosaic F0 vimentin mutants generated using CRISPR-Cas9 displayed reduced regenerate area at 3 dpw.
claims.source: The mosaic F0 mutants also displayed reduced regenerate length and area at 3 dpw (Figure 3F,G, Figure 3—figure supplement 3D, Figure 3—source data 2) but had no developmental defect in fin length (Figure 3—figure supplement 3E–G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by CRISPR-Cas9 mutagenesis data shown in Figure 3F, 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 3D, and Figure 3—source data 2.

claims.claim: Mosaic F0 vimentin mutants had no developmental defect in fin length.
claims.source: The mosaic F0 mutants also displayed reduced regenerate length and area at 3 dpw (Figure 3F,G, Figure 3—figure supplement 3D, Figure 3—source data 2) but had no developmental defect in fin length (Figure 3—figure supplement 3E–G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3E-G.

claims.claim: During regeneration of the caudal fin following amputation, the wound edge formed an uneven border that contained growing epithelial cell extensions.
claims.source: To determine how vimentin regulates wound repair, we performed long duration laser scanning confocal microscopy of wound healing dynamics. During regeneration of the caudal fin following amputation, the wound edge formed an uneven border that contained growing epithelial cell extensions (Figure 4—video 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 4—video 1.

claims.claim: The formation of epithelial extensions (projections) was not present during normal development of the caudal fin.
claims.source: The formation of these epithelial extensions, herein referred to as projections, was not present during normal development of the caudal fin, which occurred with the extension of a smooth fin edge (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The first visible projections after tail transection could be identified at 18 hpw and became prominent by 24 hpw.
claims.source: The first visible projections after tail transection could be identified at 18 hpw and became prominent by 24 hpw (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The projections continued to extend and new projections formed throughout wound repair.
claims.source: The projections continued to extend and new projections formed throughout wound repair (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Vimentin-deficient larvae possessed a smooth wound edge and relative absence of epithelial projections for more than 24 hpw.
claims.source: By contrast, vimentin-deficient larvae possessed a smooth wound edge and relative absence of the epithelial projections for more than 24 hpw (Figure 4B, Figure 4—video 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—video 2.

claims.claim: Following transection, more than 75 percent of control larvae had visible projections by 24 hpw while only about 40 percent of vimentin-deficient larvae displayed projections.
claims.source: To quantify these effects, we assessed the percentage of larvae that form visible projections. Following transection, more than 75 percent of control larvae had visible projections by 24 hpw while only about 40 percent of vimentin-deficient larvae displayed projections (Figure 4C, Figure 4—source data 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—source data 1.

claims.claim: Early pharmacological inhibition of ROS resulted in a smooth wound edge and impaired the formation of projections at 24 hpw.
claims.source: Since vimentin expression is dependent on early ROS signaling at the wound, we also characterized the effect of early ROS inhibition on the formation of epithelial projections. Early pharmacological inhibition of ROS resulted in a smooth wound edge (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) and impaired the formation of projections at 24 hpw (Figure 4D, Figure 4—source data 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, and Figure 4—source data 2.

claims.claim: Inhibition of NFκB using the small molecule WA impaired the formation of projections.
claims.source: Similar effects were observed with inhibition of NFκB using the small molecule WA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Thin finger-like projections at the wound edge extended around fibrillar proteins that protruded into the tips of the projections.
claims.source: To further characterize the epithelial projections and the role of vimentin in this process, we performed bright field imaging of the projections at high magnification. We observed thin finger-like projections at the wound edge that extended around fibrillar proteins that protruded into the tips of the projections (Figure 4E,F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by bright field imaging data shown in Figure 4E and 4F.

claims.claim: LC-PolScope microscopy suggested that the fibrillar protein in the projections was a collagen structure.
claims.source: This observation of fibrillar structures was supported by LC-PolScope microscopy (Oldenbourg, 2005) suggesting that the fibrillar protein was a collagen structure (Keikhosravi et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by LC-PolScope microscopy data and cites Oldenbourg, 2005 and Keikhosravi et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The fibers in the projections appeared to induce a physical stress on the epithelial projections, with epithelial cell membranes stretched outward around the fiber.
claims.source: These fibers appeared to induce a physical stress on the epithelial projections since the epithelial cells, whose membranes are also birefringent and can be detected with LC-PolScope microscopy, appear elongated, with the cell membranes stretched outward around the fiber (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by LC-PolScope microscopy data shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: Live SHG imaging after tail transection confirmed the presence of fibers in the projections and indicated a close association between the fibers and the projecting epithelial cells.
claims.source: To further characterize these projections, we used SHG microscopy. Live SHG imaging after tail transection confirmed the presence of fibers in the projections and indicated a close association between the fibers and the projecting epithelial cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by SHG imaging data.

claims.claim: The SHG fibers appeared to push the epithelial cells outward during extension of the wound edge.
claims.source: Notably, the SHG fibers appeared to push the epithelial cells outward during extension of the wound edge (Figure 4—video 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse SHG imaging data shown in Figure 4—video 3.

claims.claim: The SHG fibers in the caudal fin play a guidance role in the formation of epithelial projections during wound repair.
claims.source: These findings suggest that the SHG fibers in the caudal fin, which we have previously shown are important for proper wound healing (LeBert et al., 2015), play a guidance role in the formation of epithelial projections during wound repair.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that SHG fibers push epithelial cells outward, and cites LeBert et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Inhibition of projection formation in vimentin-deficient, DPI- and WA treated larvae resulted in a lack of SHG fiber-containing projections.
claims.source: Inhibition of projection formation in the vimentin-deficient, DPI- and WA treated larvae resulted in a lack of SHG fiber-containing projections as indicated by polarization imaging (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, F and H) and SHG imaging in combination with phalloidin staining (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, G and I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by polarization and SHG imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D-I.

claims.claim: Fiber projections at the wound edge were reduced in vimentin-deficient larvae.
claims.source: Since the depletion of vimentin reduced the appearance of epithelial projections (Figure 4B,C), we investigated the effect of vimentin depletion on SHG fibers. We found that fiber projections at the wound edge were reduced in vimentin-deficient larvae (Figure 5A,D, Figure 5—videos 1–4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by SHG imaging data shown in Figure 5A, 5D, and Figure 5—videos 1-4.

claims.claim: Vimentin-deficient larvae had a reduced contour length at the wound edges compared to control larvae.
claims.source: To quantify this, the length of the wound edge (contour) in SHG images of the region immediately adjacent to the end of the notochord was measured in control and vimentin-depleted larvae (Figure 5B and E). The vimentin-deficient larvae had a reduced contour length at the wound edges as compared to control larvae (Figure 5G, Figure 5—source data 1), supporting the hypothesis that the fiber projections, as well as the epithelial projections, as assessed by bright field imaging, require vimentin.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative contour length measurements shown in Figure 5G and Figure 5—source data 1.

claims.claim: Fiber projections and epithelial projections require vimentin.
claims.source: The vimentin-deficient larvae had a reduced contour length at the wound edges as compared to control larvae (Figure 5G, Figure 5—source data 1), supporting the hypothesis that the fiber projections, as well as the epithelial projections, as assessed by bright field imaging, require vimentin.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that vimentin depletion reduces both fiber and epithelial projections.

claims.claim: Fibers in vimentin-depleted fins tended to be less perpendicular overall to the wound edge than their control counterparts.
claims.source: Because our previous work indicates that SHG fiber organization plays an important role in re-growth of the transected tail fin (LeBert et al., 2015), we sought to further examine how vimentin depletion impacts SHG fiber organization. Visual observation of the control MO and vimentin MO wounded caudal fins suggested that fibers in the vimentin-depleted fins did not project perpendicularly outward and were prone to be more tangential to the wound edge. To quantify this observation we utilized CurveAlign analysis (Bredfeldt et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2017; Schneider et al., 2013) of the SHG images of the transected tails to determine the angle of the fibers relative to the wound edge (Figure 5C and F). This analysis revealed that the population of fibers with vimentin depletion tended to be less perpendicular overall than their control counterparts (Figure 5H, Figure 5—souce data 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by CurveAlign analysis shown in Figure 5H and Figure 5—source data 2, and cites Bredfeldt et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2017; Schneider et al., 2013 and LeBert et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Inhibition of early ROS signaling impaired SHG fiber contour length at 24 hpw.
claims.source: To determine if early ROS signaling also affected SHG projections we performed a similar analysis in the presence and absence of DPI. Inhibition of early ROS signaling impaired SHG fiber contour length at 24 hpw (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) as compared to controls.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by SHG imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: WA treatment impaired SHG fiber contour length at 24 hpw.
claims.source: A similar outcome was observed with WA treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by SHG imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Early wound signaling through ROS regulates vimentin expression and the subsequent formation of fiber projections during wound healing.
claims.source: Taken together, these findings suggest that early wound signaling through ROS regulates vimentin expression and the subsequent formation of fiber projections during wound healing.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results showing ROS regulates vimentin and fiber projections.

claims.claim: Collagen fibers support the movement of epithelial cell projections to promote wound edge progression during wound healing.
claims.source: These fibers support the movement of epithelial cell projections to promote wound edge progression during the process of wound healing.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that collagen fibers guide epithelial projections.

claims.claim: The caudal fin of larval zebrafish contains structural components identified as actinotrichia that are composed of both col1a1 and col2a1b.
claims.source: The caudal fin of the larval zebrafish contains structural components identified as actinotrichia (Dane and Tucker, 1985) that are composed of both col1a1 and col2a1b (Durán et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim cites Dane and Tucker, 1985 and Durán et al., 2011 as support.

claims.claim: Unwounded fins displayed a highly structured organization exhibiting both SHG and Col II antibody label.
claims.source: To confirm that the fibers we observed were composed of multiple types of collagen, we performed SHG to visualize type I/III collagen (Campagnola et al., 2002; Mohler et al., 2003) and antibody labeling of type II collagen (Col II) by immunofluorescence. Unwounded fins displayed a highly structured organization exhibiting both SHG and Col II antibody label (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by SHG and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6A, and cites Campagnola et al., 2002; Mohler et al., 2003.

claims.claim: Following amputation, the ordered orientation of collagen fibers was lost in regions adjacent to the amputated plane.
claims.source: Following amputation, this ordered orientation of fibers was lost in regions adjacent to the amputated plane (Figure 6B), however both SHG fibers and Col II labeling still associated in projections and disrupted fibers.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by SHG and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Both SHG fibers and Col II labeling still associated in projections and disrupted fibers after amputation.
claims.source: Following amputation, this ordered orientation of fibers was lost in regions adjacent to the amputated plane (Figure 6B), however both SHG fibers and Col II labeling still associated in projections and disrupted fibers.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by SHG and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Strong Col II labeling was observed at the tips of broken SHG fibers.
claims.source: Interestingly, we observed strong Col II labeling at the tips of broken SHG fibers (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: SHG fibers associate with Col II fibers during repair.
claims.source: Regardless, the findings suggest that the SHG fibers associate with Col II fibers during repair.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that SHG and Col II labeling colocalize in projections.

claims.claim: col1a1 expression increased in the wounded caudal fin by 24 hpw.
claims.source: Since previous studies suggested that vimentin regulates collagen accumulation after wounding in mouse models (Cheng et al., 2016), we wanted to determine whether the effects of vimentin on collagen fibers were due, at least in part, to changes in collagen expression. The major fibrillar collagens of the developing caudal fin are col1a1 and col2a1b (Durán et al., 2011). Therefore, we performed quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) to assess expression of col1a1 and col2a1b following caudal fin amputation. To accurately assess the expression at the site of the wound, an approximately 500 µm length of fin was collected from amputated and age-matched unwounded larvae (Figure 6C). At 24 hpw, we found an increase in col1a1 and col2a1b expression in the fins of wounded larvae (Figure 6D, Figure 6—source data 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—source data 1, and cites Cheng et al., 2016 and Durán et al., 2011.

claims.claim: col2a1b expression increased in the wounded caudal fin by 24 hpw.
claims.source: At 24 hpw, we found an increase in col1a1 and col2a1b expression in the fins of wounded larvae (Figure 6D, Figure 6—source data 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—source data 1.

claims.claim: In vitro studies in mice show that expression of collagen I is regulated by vimentin via stabilization of collagen I mRNA.
claims.source: In vitro studies in mice show that expression of collagen I is regulated by vimentin via stabilization of collagen I mRNA (Challa and Stefanovic, 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim cites Challa and Stefanovic, 2011 as support.

claims.claim: Vimentin-deficient larvae displayed a reduction in col1a1 expression at 24 hpw compared to controls.
claims.source: To determine if vimentin regulates collagen expression in our in vivo model as well, we performed qRT-PCR in vimentin-deficient larvae. At 24 hpw, vimentin-deficient larvae displayed a reduction in col1a1 and col2a1b expression at 24 hpw compared to controls (Figure 6E, Figure 6—source data 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—source data 2.

claims.claim: Vimentin-deficient larvae displayed a reduction in col2a1b expression at 24 hpw compared to controls.
claims.source: At 24 hpw, vimentin-deficient larvae displayed a reduction in col1a1 and col2a1b expression at 24 hpw compared to controls (Figure 6E, Figure 6—source data 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—source data 2.

claims.claim: Pharmacological inhibition of early ROS signaling caused a significant reduction in the rise of collagen expression following amputation at 24 hpw.
claims.source: Furthermore, pharmacological inhibition of early ROS signaling was sufficient to cause a significant reduction in the rise of collagen expression following amputation at 24 hpw (Figure 6F, Figure 6—source data 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—source data 3.

claims.claim: WA treatment caused a reduction in col1a1 and col2a1b expression at 24 hpw.
claims.source: A similar result was also observed with WA treatment (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), which may be working either through NFκB inhibition or by affecting vimentin directly.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: In vitro analysis suggests that vimentin regulates col1 expression through an interaction with La Ribonucleoprotein Domain Family Member 6 (Larp6).
claims.source: In vitro analysis of vimentin regulation of collagen expression has suggested that vimentin regulates col1 expression through an interaction with La Ribonucleoprotein Domain Family Member 6 (Larp6) (Challa and Stefanovic, 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim cites Challa and Stefanovic, 2011 as support.

claims.claim: Larp6-deficient larvae have reduced col1a1 expression but no defect in col2a1b expression.
claims.source: To determine whether this interaction also occurred in our in vivo model, we performed morpholino knockdown of larp6 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B) followed by qRT-PCR analysis at 24 hpw. We determined that Larp6-deficient larvae have reduced col1a1 expression but no defect in col2a1b expression, consistent with the published in vitro data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Larp6-deficient larvae displayed a significant defect in regenerate area at 3 dpw.
claims.source: Furthermore, Larp6-deficient larvae displayed a significant defect in regenerate area at 3 dpw, although no defect in regenerate length (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that vimentin is influencing wound healing through multiple pathways.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by regeneration measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Larp6-deficient larvae showed no defect in regenerate length at 3 dpw.
claims.source: Furthermore, Larp6-deficient larvae displayed a significant defect in regenerate area at 3 dpw, although no defect in regenerate length (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that vimentin is influencing wound healing through multiple pathways.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by regeneration measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Vimentin is influencing wound healing through multiple pathways.
claims.source: Furthermore, Larp6-deficient larvae displayed a significant defect in regenerate area at 3 dpw, although no defect in regenerate length (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that vimentin is influencing wound healing through multiple pathways.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Larp6 depletion only partially recapitulates the vimentin depletion phenotype.

claims.claim: Constant inhibition of lysyl oxidase throughout the wound healing process caused a significant reduction in regeneration of the larval fin at 2 dpw.
claims.source: Our findings suggest that vimentin affects wound healing, at least in part through affecting collagen fiber extensions and the formation of epithelial projections at the wound edge. To determine if perturbing collagen cross linking affects the formation of projections and wound repair, we used a pharmacological inhibitor of lysyl oxidase, beta aminopropionitrile (BAPN) to inhibit collagen I cross-linking and the formation of collagen I fibrils (Kagan and Li, 2003; Pinnell and Martin, 1968; Tang et al., 1983; Wilmarth and Froines, 1992). Constant inhibition of lysyl oxidase throughout the wound healing process caused a significant reduction in regeneration of the larval fin at 2 dpw (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by regeneration measurements shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-C, and cites Kagan and Li, 2003; Pinnell and Martin, 1968; Tang et al., 1983; Wilmarth and Froines, 1992.

claims.claim: BAPN treatment caused an increase in contour length over control.
claims.source: We next performed SHG imaging to determine if a defect in collagen fiber projections was also present. Interestingly, BAPN treatment caused an increase in contour length over control (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D,E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by SHG imaging data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D and 1E.

claims.claim: BAPN treatment caused a significant decrease in SHG fiber mean angle, consistent with vimentin-deficient larvae.
claims.source: However, the BAPN treatment caused a significant decrease in SHG fiber mean angle, consistent with vimentin-deficient larvae (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F) and indicates a disruption in fiber organization.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by SHG imaging analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: BAPN treatment indicates a disruption in fiber organization.
claims.source: However, the BAPN treatment caused a significant decrease in SHG fiber mean angle, consistent with vimentin-deficient larvae (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F) and indicates a disruption in fiber organization.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the decrease in SHG fiber mean angle.

claims.claim: Collagen cross-linking mediates regeneration of the fin and reorganization of collagen at the wound edge.
claims.source: Taken together, these findings suggest that collagen cross-linking mediates regeneration of the fin and reorganization of collagen at the wound edge.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the BAPN treatment results showing effects on regeneration and fiber organization.

claims.claim: Burn wound caused significant damage to the integrity of the SHG fibers near the wound edge such that fibers were absent from the region adjacent to the wound.
claims.source: To further study the connection between the formation of epithelial projections, collagen fiber extensions and healing outcome, we utilized a new zebrafish burn wound assay. Using short bursts of stimulation from a cauterizing wire, we generated a wound to the caudal fin epithelium that also caused significant damage to the integrity of the SHG fibers near the wound edge (Figure 7A) such that fibers were absent from the region adjacent to the wound.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by SHG imaging data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: A striking absence of fibers in the region near the wound edge was observed in burned caudal fins at 24 hr post burn.
claims.source: We performed SHG imaging on phalloidin labeled samples 24 hr post burn (hpb) and again observed a striking absence of fibers in the region near the wound edge in the burned caudal fins (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by SHG imaging data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Burn wounds resulting in a loss of SHG fiber integrity led to a significant reduction in the percentage of larvae displaying epithelial projections at 24 hpb compared to amputated fins.
claims.source: To determine if fins experiencing a burn wound and subsequent loss of collagen fiber integrity along the wound edge impacted healing dynamics, we compared burned caudal fins to age-matched, caudal fin-amputated larvae (Figure 7C). Compared to amputated fins, burn wounds resulting in a loss of SHG fiber integrity led to a significant reduction in the percentage of larvae displaying epithelial projections at 24 hpb (Figure 7D, Figure 7—source data 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—source data 1.

claims.claim: Burn wounds had significant defects in healing as compared to tail transection when assessed between 24 and 48 hr post injury.
claims.source: Furthermore, when we assessed the wound healing (length and area) of individual larvae between 24 and 48 hr post burn or post amputation, the burn wound had significant defects in healing as compared to tail transection (Figure 7E, Figure 7—source data 2, Figure 7—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative healing measurements shown in Figure 7E, Figure 7—source data 2, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: vim+ cells appeared at the wound edge in the burn wound, although the morphology of the cells were different compared to tail transection.
claims.source: Interestingly, vim+ cells also appeared at the wound edge in the burn wound, although the morphology of the cells were different compared to tail transection (Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 7F.

claims.claim: The formation of collagen projections at the wound edge is necessary for the formation of epithelial extensions and efficient wound repair.
claims.source: Taken together, these data suggest that the formation of collagen projections at the wound edge is necessary for the formation of epithelial extensions and efficient wound repair.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the burn wound results showing that disruption of collagen impairs epithelial projections and healing.

claims.claim: Vimentin functions downstream of wound-induced redox signaling and regulates collagen expression and reorganization during wound repair.
claims.source: In this study, we demonstrated that vimentin functions downstream of wound-induced redox signaling and regulates collagen expression and reorganization during wound repair.
claims.evidence: The claim summarizes the main findings of the study.

claims.claim: Collagen projections at the wound edge guide epithelial growth during fin regeneration, a process dependent on vimentin.
claims.source: Using live imaging, our work uncovered a previously unknown mechanism whereby collagen projections at the wound edge guide epithelial growth during fin regeneration, a process dependent on vimentin.
claims.evidence: The claim summarizes a key finding of the study.

claims.claim: In response to wounding, cells at the wound edge turn on vimentin expression and are critical for an increase in collagen expression and subsequent collagen reorganization at the wound that promotes proper tissue repair.
claims.source: In response to wounding, cells at the wound edge turn on vimentin expression and are critical for an increase in collagen expression and subsequent collagen reorganization at the wound that promotes proper tissue repair.
claims.evidence: The claim summarizes a key finding of the study.

claims.claim: vim+ cells affect the behavior of adjacent tissues by regulating the scaffold needed for regenerative outgrowth through the polarized formation of epithelial membrane extensions.
claims.source: This finding suggests that vim+ cells affect the behavior of adjacent tissues by regulating the scaffold needed for regenerative outgrowth through the polarized formation of epithelial membrane extensions.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that vim+ cells regulate collagen which guides epithelial projections.

claims.claim: Direct disruption of collagen organization by burn wound impairs the formation of the projections and subsequent regrowth.
claims.source: Further, direct disruption of collagen organization by burn wound impairs the formation of the projections and subsequent regrowth.
claims.evidence: The claim summarizes the burn wound findings.

claims.claim: vim+ cells in the fin are critical to generate a wound microenvironment that optimizes for efficient wound healing in zebrafish larvae.
claims.source: Our findings suggest that vim+ cells are critical to generate a wound microenvironment that optimizes for efficient wound healing in zebrafish larvae.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the overall findings of the study.

claims.claim: Vimentin regulates collagen mRNA through Larp6.
claims.source: Vimentin regulates collagen mRNA through Larp6 (Challa and Stefanovic, 2011) and was also shown to regulate collagen accumulation at the wound in mouse models (Cheng et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim cites Challa and Stefanovic, 2011 as support.

claims.claim: Vimentin regulates collagen accumulation at the wound in mouse models.
claims.source: Vimentin regulates collagen mRNA through Larp6 (Challa and Stefanovic, 2011) and was also shown to regulate collagen accumulation at the wound in mouse models (Cheng et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim cites Cheng et al., 2016 as support.

claims.claim: Vimentin plays a critical role in both collagen expression and its dynamic reorganization during the repair process in zebrafish larvae.
claims.source: Herein, we support, and extend, the evidence of these previous studies by showing a critical role for vimentin in both collagen expression and its dynamic reorganization during the repair process in zebrafish larvae.
claims.evidence: The claim summarizes the contribution of the study to existing knowledge.

claims.claim: Injury-induced ROS is a key player in modulating tissue regeneration.
claims.source: Substantial evidence implicates injury-induced ROS as a key player in modulating tissue regeneration.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: ROS regulates growth factor pathways such as Wnt/fgf signaling after amputation in Xenopus tadpoles.
claims.source: Prior studies indicate ROS regulates growth factor pathways such as Wnt/fgf signaling after amputation in Xenopus tadpoles (Love et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim cites Love et al., 2013 as support.

claims.claim: ROS stimulates vimentin expression in a population of cells at the wound through its effects on NFκB activity.
claims.source: We propose that ROS stimulates vimentin expression in a population of cells at the wound through its effects on NFκB activity.
claims.evidence: The claim is a proposed mechanism based on the study's findings.

claims.claim: NFκB is a redox sensitive transcription factor.
claims.source: NFκB is known to be a redox sensitive transcription factor (Nakajima and Kitamura, 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim cites Nakajima and Kitamura, 2013 as support.

claims.claim: Wound induced activation of DUOX1 and the generation of hydrogen peroxide is critical for the activation of NFκB reporter activity in zebrafish larvae.
claims.source: Moreover, wound induced activation of DUOX1 and the generation of hydrogen peroxide appears to be critical for the activation of NFκB reporter activity in zebrafish larvae (de Oliveira et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim cites de Oliveira et al., 2014 as support.

claims.claim: Redox signaling may have beneficial effects on the ECM in the wound microenvironment to promote wound healing in zebrafish.
claims.source: Moreover, these findings, in combination with published work, suggest that redox signaling may have beneficial effects on the ECM in the wound microenvironment to promote wound healing in zebrafish.
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the study's findings and published work.

claims.claim: Long-term time-lapse imaging of SHG and epithelial cell dynamics demonstrated a close association between the extending SHG filaments and the epithelial cell projections.
claims.source: Long-term time-lapse imaging of SHG and epithelial cell dynamics demonstrated a close association between the extending SHG filaments and the epithelial cell projections.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data.

claims.claim: Collagen projections guide epithelial membrane extensions during wound repair.
claims.source: This imaging supports a role for these collagen projections in guiding the epithelial membrane extensions.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the time-lapse imaging observations.

claims.claim: The absence of projections when collagen cross-linking was impaired supports a key role for these structures in tissue guidance.
claims.source: The absence of projections when collagen cross-linking was impaired supports a key role for these structures in tissue guidance.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the BAPN treatment results.

claims.claim: The localized caudal fin burn wound led to a complete loss in SHG signal in the wound margin.
claims.source: Further support for a role of these SHG fibers in tissue guidance and wound healing was based on our findings with caudal fin burn wounds. The localized caudal fin burn wound led to a complete loss in SHG signal in the wound margin.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by SHG imaging data from burn wounds.

claims.claim: The burn wound response was surprisingly different from the wound ECM response in the tail transection model.
claims.source: This burn wound response was surprisingly different from the wound ECM response in the well-studied tail transection model and makes it a unique model for future studies.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on comparison of burn wound and tail transection data.

claims.claim: Thermal damage abrogated epithelial projections and significantly impaired regeneration and repair of the fin.
claims.source: This type of thermal damage abrogated epithelial projections and significantly impaired regeneration and repair of the fin in the time frame examined.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by burn wound experimental data.

claims.claim: Fin growth during normal development does not exhibit collagen guidance, but rather progresses as a smooth surface without projections.
claims.source: It is also relevant to highlight that fin growth during normal development does not exhibit this type of collagen guidance, but rather progresses as a smooth surface without projections.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data comparing wounded and unwounded fins.

claims.claim: Collagen can promote wound healing in some contexts.
claims.source: These findings highlight the key role for collagen as a guidance cue that can promote wound healing in some contexts. In agreement with this idea substantial clinical efforts have focused on utilizing collagen scaffoldings with promising results (Kim et al., 2016; Reilly et al., 2017; Tracy et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the study's findings and cites Kim et al., 2016; Reilly et al., 2017; Tracy et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Caudal fin transection induces a ROS mediated program leading to a collagen matrix organization that guides epithelial behavior and wound repair.
claims.source: Taken together, our findings suggest that caudal fin transection induces a ROS mediated program leading to a collagen matrix organization that guides epithelial behavior and wound repair.
claims.evidence: The claim summarizes the overall findings of the study.

claims.claim: The vim+ cell population did not migrate during wound healing but rather regulated the wound microenvironment to promote efficient regeneration.
claims.source: Key to this work was the ability to live image the process of wound healing over extended durations. Using a new reporter of vim+ mesenchymal cells our findings revealed that this cell population did not migrate during wound healing but rather regulated the wound microenvironment to promote efficient regeneration.
claims.evidence: The claim summarizes a key finding from live imaging studies.

claims.claim: Collagen structure using SHG and epithelial cell membranes were imaged long term in vivo for the first time, allowing the identification of dynamic cell projections that occur during fin growth after injury.
claims.source: To our knowledge, this was the first time that collagen structure using SHG and epithelial cell membranes were imaged long term in vivo, allowing the identification of these dynamic cell projections that occur during fin growth after injury.
claims.evidence: The claim states a novel contribution of the study.

claims.claim: Zebrafish may be a powerful tool to identify new mechanisms that regulate collagen re-organization.
claims.source: This type of study highlights the power of zebrafish for imaging dynamic processes over time in vivo to uncover new mechanisms of regulation. However, a caveat is that it remains unclear how these observations translate to mammalian wound healing. As cutaneous wounds are a worldwide clinical problem, the findings suggest the possibility that zebrafish may be a powerful tool to identify new mechanisms that regulate collagen re-organization, guiding future development of therapeutics focused on optimal repair of different types of wounds, including mechanical injury and burn wounds.
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculation about the potential utility of zebrafish as a model system.

results.result: A transgenic zebrafish line Tg(−2vim:egfp) was generated to report vimentin promoter activity. The reporter shows expression consistent with published in situ hybridization patterns and responds to oncogenic HRasV12 overexpression.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 and C6 provide converging evidence from imaging data (Figures 1A-G), comparison to published expression patterns (C3), and functional validation with oncogenic Ras (C6, Figures 1H-I). The reporter line appears to faithfully recapitulate vimentin expression.

results.result: Following tail transection, vimentin expression is induced at the wound edge by 20-26 hpw in a non-motile population of cells that do not appear to arise from epithelial cells or migrate from surrounding tissue.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C12 are supported by in situ hybridization (Figure 2A-C) and time-lapse imaging (Figure 2D-G, videos). The non-motile nature is demonstrated by long-duration imaging (C11, Figure 2—video 1), and epithelial origin is excluded by live imaging (C12, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-C).

results.result: Immune cells are not involved directly or indirectly in vimentin expression at the wound edge, as vim+ cells do not colocalize with macrophage markers and their presence is unaffected by leukocyte depletion.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C15 are supported by imaging showing lack of colocalization with macrophage markers (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) and pu.1 morpholino experiments (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E). The inference that immune cells are not involved (C15) is reasonable given these negative results.

results.result: Early ROS signaling, likely through NFκB activity, regulates vimentin promoter activation at the wound edge. Inhibition of ROS (DPI treatment or Duox1 depletion) or NFκB (WA treatment) for 1 hr before and after wounding impairs vim+ cell appearance at 1 dpw.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C21 and C23 are supported by experimental data (Figures 2H-J, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-I). However, C22 notes that WA can directly inhibit vimentin protein, confounding interpretation of C21. The proposed mechanism (C23) linking ROS→NFκB→vimentin is plausible but relies on indirect evidence and cited literature (C19, C20) rather than direct demonstration of the pathway.

results.result: vim+ cells show tight association with SHG-detected collagen fibers. In unwounded fins, vim+ cells are elongated and aligned with organized fibers, while in wounded fins, rounded vim+ cells associate with misaligned fibers and elongated cells with intact fibers.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C27 are supported by SHG imaging data (Figures 2K-N, videos 3-4). The correlation between vim+ cell morphology and collagen fiber organization is clearly demonstrated, supporting the inference of association (C27).

results.result: Vimentin is required for optimal wound healing in zebrafish larvae. Vimentin-deficient larvae (morpholino or CRISPR) show reduced regenerate area and length at 3 dpw without developmental defects or changes in apoptosis. The defect is rescued by vimentin RNA co-injection.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C41 are well-supported by multiple lines of evidence: morpholino knockdown (Figure 3A-B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), CRISPR mutagenesis (Figure 3C-G), rescue experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A-C), and controls showing wound-specificity (C31, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F-H) and no apoptosis defect (C35-C36, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B). The convergence of morpholino, CRISPR, and rescue data strongly supports the conclusion.

results.result: During wound healing, epithelial projections form at the wound edge starting at 18 hpw and becoming prominent by 24 hpw. These projections are absent during normal development and are significantly reduced in vimentin-deficient larvae.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C47 are supported by time-lapse imaging (Figure 4A-B, videos 1-2) and quantification (Figure 4C). The temporal dynamics are well-documented, and the vimentin-dependence is demonstrated by reduced projection frequency in morphants (~40% vs ~75% in controls).

results.result: Early ROS inhibition (DPI) or NFκB inhibition (WA) impairs the formation of epithelial projections at 24 hpw.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C49 are supported by experimental data (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-C). However, the interpretation of WA effects is complicated by its direct inhibition of vimentin protein (C22), making it unclear whether the effect is through NFκB or vimentin.

results.result: Epithelial projections contain collagen fibers that extend into projection tips and appear to guide epithelial cell extensions. SHG fibers push epithelial cells outward during wound edge extension, and these fiber-containing projections are absent in vimentin-deficient, DPI-, and WA-treated larvae.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C56 are supported by multiple imaging modalities: bright field (Figure 4E-F), LC-PolScope (Figure 4G), SHG (Figure 4H, video 3), and combined SHG/phalloidin or SHG/GFP imaging (Figure 4H-I, video 4). The guidance role (C55) is a reasonable inference from the time-lapse data showing fibers pushing cells outward (C54). The absence of projections in treated larvae (C56) is documented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D-I.

results.result: Vimentin depletion reduces SHG fiber projections at the wound edge, decreases wound contour length, and causes fibers to be less perpendicular to the wound edge compared to controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C60 are supported by SHG imaging (Figure 5A, D, videos 1-4) and quantitative analysis using contour length measurements (Figure 5B, E, G) and CurveAlign fiber angle analysis (Figure 5C, F, H). The statistical significance is reported for both metrics.

results.result: Early ROS signaling regulates vimentin expression and the subsequent formation of fiber projections during wound healing. These collagen fibers support epithelial cell projection movement to promote wound edge progression.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C64 are supported by SHG imaging showing that DPI and WA treatment impair fiber contour length (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B). The integrative conclusion (C63-C64) is a reasonable synthesis of the ROS→vimentin→collagen→epithelial projection pathway demonstrated across multiple experiments.

results.result: The caudal fin contains actinotrichia composed of col1a1 and col2a1b. SHG fibers (type I/III collagen) and Col II antibody labeling show tight association in unwounded fins and continue to associate in projections after amputation, with strong Col II labeling at tips of broken SHG fibers.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C70 are supported by SHG and immunofluorescence imaging (Figure 6A-B). C65 cites published literature for actinotrichia composition. The colocalization of SHG and Col II is clearly shown, and the Col II caps at fiber tips (C69) are an interesting observation, though their function remains unclear as noted in the text.

results.result: Wounding induces increased col1a1 and col2a1b expression by 24 hpw. This increase is reduced in vimentin-deficient larvae and by early ROS inhibition (DPI) or WA treatment.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C72, C74-C77 are supported by qRT-PCR data (Figure 6D-F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A). Statistical significance is reported for the wound-induced increase and the reductions with vimentin depletion and inhibitor treatments. The data consistently show vimentin and ROS regulate collagen expression.

results.result: Vimentin regulates col1a1 expression through Larp6, as shown by in vitro studies and confirmed in vivo. Larp6-deficient larvae show reduced col1a1 but not col2a1b expression, and have defects in regenerate area but not length, suggesting vimentin influences wound healing through multiple pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C73 and C78 cite published in vitro work. Claims C79-C82 are supported by morpholino knockdown and qRT-PCR (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B-C) and regeneration measurements (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D). The partial phenotype of Larp6 depletion (area but not length defect) compared to vimentin depletion supports the inference of multiple pathways (C82).

results.result: Inhibition of collagen cross-linking with BAPN reduces fin regeneration at 2 dpw and disrupts fiber organization, causing increased contour length but decreased fiber mean angle (more parallel to wound edge), indicating disrupted fiber organization.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C87 are supported by regeneration measurements (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-C) and SHG analysis (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D-F). However, the authors note potential toxicity issues and that the increased contour length (C84) may be an artifact of measurement technique due to V-shaped fin morphology. The interpretation is further complicated by the inability to extend experiments to 3 dpw due to lethality.

results.result: Burn wounds cause loss of SHG fiber integrity at the wound edge, leading to reduced epithelial projections and impaired healing compared to tail transection. vim+ cells still appear but with different morphology.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C93 are supported by SHG imaging (Figure 7A-B), quantification of projections (Figure 7D) and healing (Figure 7E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1G), and vim+ cell imaging (Figure 7F). The burn model provides strong evidence that collagen fiber integrity is necessary for projection formation and efficient healing (C93).

results.result: The study demonstrates that vimentin functions downstream of wound-induced ROS signaling to regulate collagen expression and reorganization. Collagen projections guide epithelial growth during regeneration, and vim+ cells regulate the wound microenvironment to promote efficient healing.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C97, C99, C102, and C117 represent integrative conclusions synthesizing the major findings. These are well-supported by the collective evidence from ROS inhibition, vimentin depletion, collagen analysis, and burn wound experiments. The pathway ROS→vimentin→collagen→epithelial projections→healing is demonstrated through multiple complementary approaches.

results.result: The study proposes that ROS stimulates vimentin expression through NFκB activity, linking early wound signaling to ECM organization. This may have beneficial effects on wound healing in zebrafish.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C104 cite established knowledge. Claims C105-C108 represent proposed mechanisms and speculation. While C106-C107 cite supporting literature, the direct demonstration of the ROS→NFκB→vimentin pathway in this system is incomplete. C108 is explicitly speculative about beneficial effects of redox signaling.

results.result: Long-term time-lapse imaging demonstrates that collagen projections guide epithelial extensions during wound repair. Disruption of collagen organization (by cross-linking inhibition or burn injury) impairs projections and healing. This guidance mechanism is wound-specific and not present during normal development.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C116 synthesize imaging and experimental evidence. The guidance role (C110) is supported by time-lapse data. The importance of collagen organization is demonstrated by BAPN treatment (C111) and burn wounds (C112-C114). The wound-specificity (C115) is shown by comparison to normal development. C116 appropriately contextualizes findings with clinical literature.

results.result: The study used long-term in vivo imaging of collagen (SHG) and epithelial cells to identify dynamic projections during wound healing. The vim+ cell population is non-motile but regulates the wound microenvironment. Zebrafish may be a powerful tool for identifying mechanisms of collagen reorganization.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C119 accurately describe methodological contributions and key findings. C120 is speculative about future utility but appropriately caveated regarding translation to mammalian systems. The imaging approach is indeed novel and well-executed.
